rv.q: The despair of being bullied is one theme of Nick Payne's clever, edgy domestic drama, "If There Is I Haven't Found It Yet," about a British family that knows it's falling apart but can't seem to take action to stop it. Kudos to Beowulf Boritt for set design, and to the whole production crew for creating major watery magic.

When a little orphan hit machine named "Annie" opened in 1977, Americans living in shacks seemed positively Dickensian. Nobody had said anything about federal works projects for decades, much less offered a big wet kiss for the New Deal and sang about it in a sunny musical comedy.

So it is with this handsome revival, infinitely superior to the previous Broadway incarnation, a woefully bedraggled 1997 staging with Nell Carter as orphanage monster Miss Hannigan that ran for only 239 performances.
You will cry, or consider crying, if you have a functioning amygdala.
Overall results suggest a family crowdpleaser, at least until the potential competition when the little-girl-centric Brit hit “Matilda” comes to town in the spring.
But once you start to think of Warbucks as a real person, his blossoming love for little Annie can register as a bit creepy in the age of “Law and Order: Special Victims Unit.”
This version, which flirts with shadows, moves more shakily.
It is an odd thing indeed to watch Sandy get a huge ovation from New Yorkers.
The new production of 'Annie' is a slick, professionally executed revival that hits all the familiar marks without adding anything particularly fresh or memorable to the mix.
Returning to Broadway almost three decades later, this enduring ode to optimism remains a sterling example of expert musical-theater craftsmanship.
If this take seldom crosses the line into something must-see special (it doesn’t), even a simply good production of “Annie” offers rewards.

cn.t: This revival of the Depression-era musical arrives with timely optimism and handsome production values, though critics find it serviceable rather than inspired, hitting familiar marks without adding much freshness to the beloved crowdpleaser.
